title: The Diversification Lie Draining Your Money

beats.say: Owning twenty different funds doesn't mean your hard-earned money is safe.
beats.visual: Low angle, silhouette of a lone figure standing on the edge of a wet concrete rooftop overlooking an endless grid of dark skyscrapers during blue hour, dense fog cutting across the skyline.

beats.say: Most investors buy five separate index funds, assuming they've spread their risk across the market.
beats.visual: Extreme wide, tiny human silhouette walking past massive concrete support pillars beneath a highway underpass, harsh sodium light casting sharp diagonal shadows on damp ground.

beats.say: So why does a single market downturn still wipe out their entire portfolio?
beats.visual: High angle, lone figure in a dark coat standing motionless on a rain-slick crosswalk at night, cold fluorescent reflections streaking across wet asphalt.

beats.say: You assume you own hundreds of companies, but you really bought the same ten giants five times.
beats.visual: Extreme close-up from behind a person's shoulder, hands shuffling five identical plain matte grey ledger cards under a single practical desk lamp in a shadowy room.

beats.say: Wall Street calls this diworsification, and it silently concentrates your risk instead of spreading it.
beats.visual: Low angle, looking up at cold steel and glass towers vanishing into thick low-hanging storm clouds at dusk, lone shadowy figure standing at the plaza base.

beats.say: When your broad fund, tech fund, and growth fund hold identical shares, you aren't hedged.
beats.visual: Extreme wide shot of a vast empty container port terminal at night, rows of identical stacked steel shipping containers illuminated by towering sodium floodlights.

beats.say: You haven't built a safety net; you've just bought multiple tickets on the same sinking ship.
beats.visual: High angle, solitary figure standing on a dark wooden pier looking out over vast, turbulent open water during a cold twilight drizzle.

beats.say: Worse, overlapping specialty funds hit your balance with expensive management fees every single year.
beats.visual: Low angle, silhouette of hands untying a heavy weathered nautical rope under cold industrial fluorescent lights in an empty concrete corridor.

beats.say: $100,000 for 30 years at 7% minus a 1.00% annual fee leaves you with $574,349.
beats.visual: Extreme wide, lone person walking down an empty multi-lane highway at night, streetlights stretching into deep perspective under a starless sky.

beats.say: With a 0.05% annual fee, that exact same $100,000 grows to $750,626.
beats.visual: High angle, single practical light beam piercing pitch-black darkness, illuminating a lone pair of hands sorting smooth dark river stones on weathered dark oak.

beats.say: That overlap doesn't protect you; it just burns $176,277 in lost gains for fake safety.
beats.visual: Low angle, massive towering concrete dam wall rising into the fog, a tiny human silhouette standing at the base on wet cracked bedrock.

beats.say: Real diversification means holding different asset classes, not collecting identical stocks wrapped in separate logos.
beats.visual: Extreme wide, lone traveler standing on a high mountain ridge line at blue hour, looking down at layered mountain silhouettes fading into cold mist.

beats.say: Cut the duplicates, lower your fees, and follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: Low angle, silhouette of a person standing at the edge of an empty wet asphalt road vanishing into morning fog, amber dawn horizon cutting through mist.

caption:
Owning twenty funds isn't diversification if they all hold the exact same stocks.
